title: Install
text:
Written for version 0.1.13. Steps checked against the help pages linked under each one on 30 October 2026. Menus change; if what you see differs, tell the maintainer through a GitHub issue.
Installing the plugin gives the assistant instructions only. It grants no access to data, to your GitHub account or to anything on your computer.
Pick the assistant you use.

title: Install
section: Claude (on the web, the desktop app or Cowork)
text:
Claude (on the web, the desktop app or Cowork)
You need a paid Claude plan (Pro, Max, Team or Enterprise).
Add the plugin’s marketplace (a marketplace is a list of plugins kept in a GitHub repository):

In Claude, open the Customize menu in the left sidebar.
Open the Plugins tab.
Click Add, then Add marketplace.
Choose Add from a repository.
Type VagishHemmige/r-analysis-workflow and confirm.

If your organization limits which marketplaces you can add, Claude will refuse it; ask your administrator.
Install the plugin:

Still in Customize → Plugins, open the Discover tab.
Select R Analysis Workflow and click Add.

In Cowork, open the Cowork tab first, then Customize.
Once installed, it works in chat on the web, the Chat tab of the desktop app, Cowork, and Claude Code when you sign in with the same account.
Source: Anthropic, Use plugins in Claude. Not yet tried by a person with this plugin since it moved into the plugin/ folder (see VALIDATION.md).

title: Install
text:
Claude Code
You need Claude Code version 2.1.292 or later for the one-line install.
Install, in your terminal (not inside a Claude Code session):
claude plugin install r-analysis-workflow --marketplace VagishHemmige/r-analysis-workflow
It should print that it added the marketplace and then installed the plugin. To check, run claude plugin list: you should see r-analysis-workflow@r-analysis-workflow. The plugin loads the next time you start Claude Code.
On an older version, use two commands instead:
claude plugin marketplace add VagishHemmige/r-analysis-workflow
claude plugin install r-analysis-workflow@r-analysis-workflow
Updates. Claude Code does not update plugins from this marketplace automatically unless you turn it on. Either:

turn it on once: inside a Claude Code session type /plugin, go to the Marketplaces tab, select r-analysis-workflow, then select Enable auto-update; or
update by hand when you want to, in your terminal:

claude plugin update r-analysis-workflow@r-analysis-workflow
Sources: Claude Code docs, Install and manage plugins and Plugin commands reference. The install from GitHub was tested in a sandbox with Claude Code 2.1.314 (VALIDATION.md).

title: Install
text:
ChatGPT
In ChatGPT you make the plugin with OpenAI’s Plugin Creator, pointing it at this repository. Whether Plugin Creator is available depends on your plan and workspace; OpenAI’s help pages don’t list the plans.
Create the plugin:

Start a new conversation.
Type @, search for Plugin Creator, and select it.
Ask it, in your own words: Create a plugin from the plugin/ folder of https://github.com/VagishHemmige/r-analysis-workflow.
Answer its questions and follow its prompts to finish. Check that the name is R Analysis Workflow.

Use it: in a new conversation, type @, start typing “R Analysis Workflow”, and select it under Plugins.
Update it when a new version comes out:

Open Plugins and select R Analysis Workflow.
Choose Edit Plugin.
Ask it to update the plugin from the plugin/ folder of the same repository, keeping its name.

Sources: OpenAI, Build plugins (steps 1, 2 and 4, using it, and updating) and Plugins in ChatGPT.
What has and hasn’t been checked:

OpenAI’s pages describe Plugin Creator building a plugin from your description and files. They don’t describe creating one from a GitHub repository (step 3). The maintainer tried step 3 with this layout on 30 October 2026 and it worked.
Updating through Edit Plugin from the repository has not been tried with this plugin.
Uploading a ZIP of the plugin/ folder: OpenAI’s help page mentions uploading a plugin but gives no steps, and it has not been tried with this layout. GitHub’s Download ZIP button gives the whole repository, not the plugin/ folder, so it is not the right file.
Workspace administrators can import plugins from a GitHub marketplace that syncs daily, but this repository does not have the catalog file ChatGPT needs for that.

title: Runs
text:
Written for version 0.1.13. Records: testing/runs. Every person named in them is a simulated persona.
One line per run, newest first. Each record has a scorecard (what worked, what partly worked, what failed, with the evidence) and run notes (setup, environment, and anything the orchestrator got wrong).

title: Runs
section: Earlier checks without a record here
text:
Earlier checks without a record here
These are described in VALIDATION.md, but their records are not in this repository:

Blind review (Test A) of four reviewers (clinician reader, clinician-researcher, statistician, coding expert) on Cryptococcus-cost-analysis at commit 015aa6b.
Blind review of the plugin itself (0.1.7, 2026-10-26): five reviewers read only the shipped plugin and its stated principles; 46 findings, which 0.1.8 acted on.

title: How it’s tested
text:
Written for version 0.1.13. Full procedure: testing/README.md.
A plugin is a set of instructions, so testing it means watching assistants follow those instructions and checking what they actually did. Two tests do this, both run by an orchestrating agent that starts independent assistants, passes messages between them and keeps the record. Neither needs ChatGPT itself. They stand in for real use, which remains the final check.

title: How it’s tested
text:
How a run is recorded

Before a run, its starting point is written down: the plugin commit, and for a run that doesn’t start from nothing, the simulated world it starts from and every defect planted in it, with what passing looks like. These are the setups.
During a run, every gap is logged as it appears: something the plugin didn’t cover, something it made go right, or a tension between two of its rules.
After a run, the repository keeps its scorecard and run notes (environment, setup used, and anything the orchestrator got wrong). Transcripts and the gap log are working material and are kept outside the repository. Each gap still open becomes an issue on the plugin’s repository.
Then the plugin is fixed from those issues, one decision at a time by the maintainer, and the affected part is run again.

The list of runs is on Runs. What the fixes add up to is on Problems it solves.

title: How it’s tested
text:
What the tests can’t show

How ChatGPT or Claude themselves behave with the plugin installed. The assistants in the tests follow the plugin as written, in a sandbox.
What happens with real restricted data. Tests use public or made-up data only.
What happens without the plugin. No run has yet compared the same scenario without it.

title: Join or leave a project
text:
What it is for
Helping someone start contributing to a project at the level of help they want, and helping someone who is leaving hand over so the next person can carry on from the repository alone.

title: Join or leave a project
Join or leave a project
text:
Leaving
When you say you are leaving, or a check-in sees your end date coming, the assistant works through four things with you:

Documents that exist only in a chat, on your laptop or in email, moved into the repository.
Open issues and pull requests: finished, handed on, closed with a reason, or left open with a note saying what each waits on.
Requests you made that have no answer yet, recorded so they aren’t lost.
Ownership: if you own the repository, transferring it to the PI, and then fixing the website links and switching the site back on, since GitHub does not redirect the website.

Not everything has to be finished. Something left open with a clear note is fine.

title: Join or leave a project
text:
What it will not do

Require R, Git or Quarto for work that doesn’t need them.
Ask you to paste a token or password.
Change account settings, install software or publish without your say-so.

title: Join or leave a project
text:
Ask it, for example

“Explain this project’s question and show where I can help with the protocol. Assume I can’t read R.”
“I know R but not GitHub. Help me make one contribution.”
“My rotation ends Friday. Help me hand over.”

title: Review
text: Written for version 0.1.13. Full instructions: SKILL.md.

title: Review
text:
What it is for
Checking work before it is merged or made public: a single change, the plan, the website against the code, or the whole project.

title: Review
text:
When to use it

Before asking a colleague to look at a pull request.
When the plan is drafted, or before it is locked.
Before the website, tables or figures go public.
Whenever you want a second opinion on the project as it stands.

title: Review
text:
What happens
You choose the kind of review, or describe what you want checked and the assistant picks:







Review
What it checks




Change
A pull request or branch, every file it touches, against the plan and the project’s rules


Plan ↔︎ code
Every part of the plan has code, and the code settles nothing the plan leaves open


Plan
The plan is complete, its methods fit the question, and its citations say what it claims


Site ↔︎ code
The website explains the code as it is


Architecture
ARCHITECTURE.md matches the scripts


Repository
The required files, the data-sources table, .gitignore and protection of the main copy


Reporting
The flow diagram, tables, models and numbers in prose agree


Release
Nothing restricted or uncleared, no credentials, and alt text, before anything goes public; then a person signs off



Most reviews use some of five blind reviewers: a clinician reader, a clinician-researcher, a statistician, a coding expert and a librarian. Each works as a separate assistant with only the files its role needs and public material such as cited papers, without seeing the other reviewers’ findings or the conversation that produced the work. A final step checks every claimed error against the source before reporting it, and marks findings already known from issues.

title: Review
text:
What it will not do

Change anything while reviewing. Acting on the findings comes afterwards, one at a time, as you choose.
Give reviewers restricted data. Reviewers read only code, documentation and material cleared for release, so a review stays within the project’s data agreements.

title: Review
text:
Ask it, for example

“Review pull request #12 before my supervisor sees it.”
“Run a full blind review of this repository.”
“Check the site is ready to go public.”

title: Review
text:
Where the detail lives

The blind reviewers: what each reads, its prompt, and how reports are combined
Data handling, for the Release review

How the reviewers themselves are tested is on Blind review (Test A).

title: Sites built with it
text:
Written for version 0.1.13.
None are listed yet.
This page will list public project websites built with the plugin from the start. If you have built one, open an issue on the plugin’s repository with its address.
To see what a project site looks like before then, the plugin’s starter files hold a small example site with made-up code.

title: Problems it solves
text:
Written for version 0.1.13.
Each entry names a problem an analysis project can run into, the plugin rule that addresses it, the version that added the rule, and how it fared in testing. Entries are ordered by the stage of a project where the problem arises.
What this page does and doesn’t claim. It describes risks the plugin is built to handle. It does not claim what would happen without the plugin: no run has yet compared the same scenario with and without it. The test results come from simulated users (see How it’s tested). Versions before 0.1.7 are not recorded in this repository, so rules from then are marked “before 0.1.7”.
Test results use the scorecards’ scale: ✔ worked as intended, ~ worked partly or only because a person caught it, ✘ failed, not yet tested.

title: Problems it solves
text:
Getting the plugin to work

The assistant can’t open the plugin’s shared guidance

The risk: ChatGPT’s skills package only each skill’s own folder, so guidance shared between skills was out of reach and every skill ran without it.
What the plugin does: keeps one source copy of each shared file and generates a copy inside every skill that uses it (build_skills.py); the release check fails if a copy is stale.
Since: 0.1.10.
Tested: each skill folder resolves every link inside itself when copied alone; not yet tested in ChatGPT (VALIDATION.md).

title: Problems it solves
text:
Starting a project

A novice can’t get from an idea to a working repository

The risk: a student with no GitHub account and no R is asked to install tools, learn Git and set up a repository before anything useful happens.
What the plugin does: a short questionnaire, one question at a time, reusing what is already known, with no installs until the work needs them (initialize-analysis).
Since: before 0.1.7; setting up from R added in 0.1.12.
Tested: ✔ a novice went from nothing to a public repository, protected main copy, setup notes, a draft pull request and her own assistant project in one session (0.1.8 scorecard).



The main copy is unprotected, or the website never goes live

The risk: a repository’s rules say changes go through pull requests when nothing enforces it, or a site is built but never switched on.
What the plugin does: gives the maintainer the steps to protect the default branch and switch on GitHub Pages, reminds them when the first site is merged, and offers a check that reads the actual settings rather than assuming them (GitHub workflow).
Since: Pages reminder 0.1.7; the settings check 0.1.12.
Tested: not yet tested. The 0.1.12 check has not been run (VALIDATION.md).



Data or secrets end up in a public repository

The risk: data files, credentials or outputs not yet cleared are committed, and deleting them later doesn’t remove them from history.
What the plugin does: a .gitignore adapted to the project and reviewed before the first commit, the full file list read before committing, and steps for what to do if something was pushed by mistake (data handling).
Since: .gitignore before 0.1.7; reading the file list and the steps after a mistake 0.1.12.
Tested: the ignore rules were tested with git check-ignore in a scratch repository (VALIDATION.md).

title: Problems it solves
text:
Deciding the science

Someone settles a scientific question who shouldn’t

The risk: a student, or an assistant, quietly chooses a cut-off, covariate or exclusion in code, and nobody can later say who decided or why.
What the plugin does: the analysis plan decides; every open choice is a decision issue on GitHub settled only by a named decider; assistants draft options and never choose (analysis plan). The deciders are asked for at setup.
Since: before 0.1.7; deciders asked at setup 0.1.8.
Tested: ✔ across two student leads, an impatient statistician and a clinician who used only email (0.1.8 scorecard); ✔ through peer review six months later (continuation scorecard).



Input from a collaborator who doesn’t use GitHub is lost

The risk: a clinician’s decision arrives by email or in a meeting, lives in one person’s inbox, and is gone when they leave.
What the plugin does: whoever received it posts the decider’s exact words in the decision issue, with name, date and how it was given; a summary from memory doesn’t settle anything (analysis plan).
Since: 0.1.8.
Tested: ✔ throughout (0.1.8 scorecard). ✘ on consent: a collaborator’s whole email was posted to a public repository before she knew it was public; no rule yet covers this.



A decision is credited to the wrong person

The risk: a draft says “Dr. X decided” when Dr. X didn’t, or puts someone’s words in another’s mouth.
What the plugin does: writing that a person decided, said or wrote something needs a link to the record; if there is none, the assistant asks instead (conventions).
Since: 0.1.9.
Tested: ~ in 0.1.8, before the rule, two wrong attributions were caught only by the people concerned (continuation scorecard); ✔ in the 0.1.9 re-test, where an agreement given only verbally was not asserted (0.1.9 scorecard).



The plan changes after results are seen, without a record

The risk: a locked plan is edited once results are in, and a reader can’t tell what was planned from what was chosen afterwards.
What the plugin does: at locking, an empty “Amendments after locking” section and a tag; every later change gets a dated entry saying whether it was made before or after outcome data were seen, and a new tag (analysis plan).
Since: the amendment rule before 0.1.9; the empty section at locking 0.1.9.
Tested: ~ in 0.1.8 the rule never reached the repository and three claims about when results had been seen proved false (continuation scorecard); ✔ in the 0.1.9 re-test, the section was added at locking (0.1.9 scorecard).

title: Problems it solves
text:
Working with an assistant

Something is posted in a person’s name that they never saw

The risk: an assistant posts an issue comment, a pull-request description or an email as the person, with wording they wouldn’t have used.
What the plugin does: shows the exact text first and waits for a go-ahead, unless the person’s own instructions waive it (conventions).
Since: 0.1.7.
Tested: ~ mostly held, with two conflicts with other rules (0.1.8 scorecard); ✔ throughout the continuation, where it let a person correct the provenance of his own text before it was posted (continuation scorecard).



Work is left in a chat or a download, and lost

The risk: a new chat remembers nothing, so a draft that lives only in an old chat or a downloads folder is gone.
What the plugin does: at the end of a session, asks whether anything unfinished should be saved to the repository and offers where (conventions); a check-in looks for drafts that never got there (onboarding).
Since: 0.1.7.
Tested: ~ worked in most sessions; failed once, when prepared changes were kept as downloads and one was lost (0.1.8 scorecard).



The assistant asks too much, or too little

The risk: a novice is swamped by questions, or an assistant builds a whole setup on its own reading of the first request.
What the plugin does: how much to ask depends on the working style the person chose (review only, step by step, or hands-off), step by step when none is set, with rules that hold in every style (conventions).
Since: working styles 0.1.7; one consolidated rule 0.1.11.
Tested: not yet tested in a simulated session under each style (VALIDATION.md).



Directions to click through menus that don’t exist

The risk: an assistant describes a menu path from memory, and a novice can’t find it.
What the plugin does: use the plugin’s own steps, check the app’s current help pages, or say it isn’t sure and describe what to look for (conventions).
Since: 0.1.7.
Tested: ~ in the 0.1.9 re-test, one click path for GitHub was given with no source and not flagged as unchecked (0.1.9 scorecard).



Code written from memory for the wrong package version

The risk: code works against the version the assistant remembers, not the one installed, and fails or silently changes results.
What the plugin does: read the documentation of the installed version, including its news; test past any fake once against the real package; name the version relied on in the pull request (AGENTS.md template).
Since: 0.1.9.
Tested: ✔ read the project’s locked version and its documentation, and said plainly what it couldn’t run; ✘ the suggested pull-request text didn’t name the version (0.1.9 scorecard).



Code a clinician-analyst can’t read

The risk: assistant-written R is dense with constructs that someone who learned R from online guides can’t follow, so nobody on the team can check it.
What the plugin does: a readable-R rule for new code, and any style-only change to tested code must show identical outputs (conventions).
Since: 0.1.9.
Tested: ✔ on new code early in the continuation; not yet on a large new analysis (continuation scorecard).

title: Problems it solves
text:
Code and the website

The website stops describing the actual code

The risk: a page holds a pasted copy of code that has since changed, so readers are told the analysis does something it doesn’t.
What the plugin does: pages import labelled sections from the scripts themselves, and are updated in the same pull request as the code (document-analysis).
Since: before 0.1.7.
Tested: ✔ pages imported the real code; ~ pages went stale between pull requests (0.1.8 scorecard).



Pull requests pile up and nobody knows the merge order

The risk: a change built on another unmerged change leaves the reviewer to work out an order, and conflicts follow.
What the plugin does: every pull request is based on the default branch; a change that needs an unmerged one waits for it or is folded into it (GitHub workflow).
Since: 0.1.7.
Tested: ✔ test merges before advising; a stacked branch kept off a pull request until its base merged (0.1.8 scorecard).

title: Problems it solves
text:
Review

A review misses part of what changed

The risk: a reviewer reads the file the author mentioned and misses an unrelated file that came along in the same commit.
What the plugin does: a change review reads every file the change touches and lists them; a file not read is named, with the reason (review-analysis).
Since: 0.1.9.
Tested: ✔ in the 0.1.9 re-test, all four planted defects across five files were found, plus one that wasn’t planted (0.1.9 scorecard).



A reviewer’s claimed error isn’t real

The risk: an assistant reviewer reports a confident error that doesn’t hold, and someone acts on it.
What the plugin does: five blind reviewers, and a combining step that checks every claimed error against the source before listing it (reviewers).
Since: before 0.1.7.
Tested: ✔ in the blind review at the end of the 0.1.8 simulation, each reviewer stayed in role, unverifiable claims were marked as such, and no data rule was breached (0.1.8 scorecard). ✘ the full panel was never offered for the pull request that implemented the primary analysis.

title: Problems it solves
text:
Going public

Results go public before anyone meant them to

The risk: tables, figures or estimates reach a public repository or website before they are cleared, or before the paper.
What the plugin does: whether outputs are tracked is decided at setup and the reason recorded; no results in code, comments or other repository text; a Release review before anything goes public, then a person signs off (data handling, review-analysis).
Since: 0.1.8 to 0.1.12 (results out of repository text 0.1.8; the reason for ignoring outputs 0.1.9; the Disclosure check 0.1.12).
Tested: ~ in the continuation, outputs tracked by the project’s .gitignore would have carried real estimates to the public repository while the assistant advised keeping them off, and its own audit of what was public was incomplete (continuation scorecard).

title: Problems it solves
text:
Handing over

The next lead can’t find out where things stand

The risk: a rotating student leaves, and the next one has only a repository link and no idea what was done, decided or promised.
What the plugin does: the next person starts from the repository, not the last person’s files; leaving follows four steps (documents, open work, pending requests, ownership), started by the person or by a check-in that sees their end date (onboarding).
Since: 0.1.7.
Tested: ✔ the hand-over was started by the plugin’s own scheduled reminder, and the next lead rebuilt the state from the repository in one reply (0.1.8 scorecard).



Transferring the repository breaks the website

The risk: a student who owns the repository leaves; after the transfer the old site address stops working, because GitHub doesn’t redirect websites.
What the plugin does: raises the transfer before the student leaves, orders it last, and lists the links to update and the site to switch on again (onboarding).
Since: 0.1.7.
Tested: ~ the transfer was done in the right order, but old links were still on the site at the end (0.1.8 scorecard).

title: R Analysis Workflow
text: Written for version 0.1.13.

title: R Analysis Workflow
text:
What it is
R Analysis Workflow is a plugin for ChatGPT and Claude. A plugin is a set of instructions the assistant reads when a task calls for them, so it works the same way every time and in every chat. This one is for biomedical analyses written in R, whose code and methods are published on GitHub and explained on a website. It is not for building R packages.
With the plugin installed, you ask in plain words (“Help me start this project”, “I’m joining this project and I’m new to GitHub”) and the assistant follows the plugin’s steps.

title: R Analysis Workflow
R Analysis Workflow
section: What a project built with it has
text:
What a project built with it has

An analysis plan (analysis-plan.md) that decides the science. The code does what the plan says.
Decision issues on GitHub for each scientific question still open. Only the named deciders settle them; the assistant drafts the options and never chooses.
R code in labelled sections, with the analysis run from one script.
A website that explains each step of the code in plain language for a clinician reader. It shows the real code, and never runs the analysis.
AGENTS.md, the rules any assistant follows in that project: who decides what, which data it may never read, and how changes are made.
Pull requests for every change to the main copy, so each change can be seen and checked before it goes in.

title: R Analysis Workflow
text:
Where to start

Install the plugin.
Then, depending on what you are doing: start a project, join or leave one, explain the code, report results or review the work.
To see how the plugin is checked, read How it’s tested and Problems it solves.

title: R Analysis Workflow
text:
Before you rely on it
The plugin guides an assistant; it does not check your science. Review what the assistant produces as you would a new collaborator’s work, before it goes into a plan, a paper or a decision. VALIDATION.md lists what has and has not been tested.
The source, including every instruction the assistant reads, is on GitHub. Original text and code are MIT licensed.

title: Report results
text: Written for version 0.1.13. Full instructions: SKILL.md.

title: Report results
text:
What it is for
Building the tables, figures and numbers a paper reports, so that every count and estimate comes from the code that produced it and matches the analysis plan.

title: Report results
text:
When to use it

You are ready to build the participant flow diagram, Table 1, survival curves or model tables.
You want to check that the numbers in a draft agree with each other and with what was fitted.

title: Report results
text:
What happens
The work follows a fixed order, using the parts that fit the design:

Participant flow: the diagram of who was included and excluded, built by the same code that builds the analysis dataset (with the flowchart package), so the two can’t disagree.
Descriptions and missingness: every analysis variable, with missing values shown.
Table 1, grouped the way the plan says (with gtsummary).
Two-variable and stratified summaries, where the plan calls for them.
Repeated measurements over time, where they exist.
Time to event: follow-up, events and censoring, before any model.
Figures, following published principles for clear statistical graphics, with survival curves in the KMunicate style and rules for small counts.
Model tables that report the model actually fitted.

Before finishing it checks that every number reconciles with the flow diagram, that estimates and their labels match the fitted model, and that every number written in prose comes from a computed value, never retyped.

title: Report results
text:
What it will not do

Choose the model, covariates or how missing data are handled. Those come from the plan; an open one becomes a decision issue.
Read restricted data. It writes and tests the code on made-up data; a person with access runs it on the real data, and every output passes the project’s disclosure rules before it leaves.

title: Report results
text:
Ask it, for example

“Build Table 1 from the analysis dataset, grouped by exposure as in the plan.”
“Make the Kaplan–Meier figure with a risk table.”
“Check that the numbers in the results section match the tables.”

title: Report results
text:
Where the detail lives

Reporting guidance
Data handling

For an independent check afterwards, ask for the Reporting review (see Review).

title: Start a project
text:
What it is for
Setting up a new analysis project, or tidying an existing one (a folder of scripts, or one long R Markdown file), so it becomes a GitHub repository in a consistent layout that the next person can pick up.

title: Start a project
text:
When to use it

You have an idea, a protocol or an old script, and no repository yet.
You have a repository that grew without a plan and want it organized.
A setup was started in an earlier chat and not finished.

title: Start a project
Start a project
text:
What it will not do

Choose a scientific option. It drafts the options; a decider settles them.
Open data that may be restricted while taking stock of a folder.
Install tools, publish anything or change repository settings on its own.

title: Start a project
text:
Ask it, for example

“Set up my R analysis project from my latest RMD and protocol.”
“I have no GitHub account and no R. Help me get this project started.”
“We started setting this up last week; carry on from where it stopped.”

title: Explain the code
text: Written for version 0.1.13. Full instructions: SKILL.md.

title: Explain the code
text:
What it is for
Keeping the project’s website, README and ARCHITECTURE.md in step with the code. The website is how a clinician, a reviewer or the next student understands what the analysis does without reading R.

title: Explain the code
text:
When to use it

A script has just joined the analysis (the main script now runs it) and needs its page.
Code changed and its page should say what it does now.
A page holds a pasted copy of code that may no longer match the script.
The site, README or architecture description needs repair.
A decision was made, the plan was locked, or a new data source was added, and the plan needs updating to match.

title: Explain the code
Explain the code
text:
What it will not do

Run the analysis to build the website. Pages show code; results appear only from outputs already cleared for release.
Invent a citation. A statement that needs one it can’t find is flagged for the librarian reviewer.
Restyle an existing site without asking. It lists the differences from the plugin’s conventions first.

title: Explain the code
text:
Ask it, for example

“This page has pasted code; switch it to import from the script.”

title: User simulation (Test B)
text:
Written for version 0.1.13. Full procedure: testing/README.md, Test B. Scenario: scenario.md.
Every person in this test, and in its records, is a simulated persona played by an AI agent. None of them is a real person, and the project uses only public data.

title: User simulation (Test B)
text:
What it tests
Whether a person with no GitHub account and no R can start a project from nothing with the plugin, and whether the people who come after can pick it up from the repository alone, through to a finished, reviewed analysis.

title: User simulation (Test B)
text:
The project
A new observational analysis: is an elevated level of serum free light chains associated with death from any cause, independent of age, sex and kidney function? It uses the public flchain dataset from the R survival package, which needs no data agreement.

title: User simulation (Test B)
text:
The roles in a run

Assistant: stands in for ChatGPT with the plugin installed. A fresh one for every session, because a new chat remembers nothing. It follows only the plugin. Its brief: assistant-brief.md.
Personas: one per person, kept across that person’s sessions, because people remember even when chats don’t. A persona never sees the plugin and writes only what the person would type.
Check-in: stands in for a scheduled task, run fresh each time it is due, reporting what is waiting on its person.
Orchestrator: passes messages word for word, carries out website actions a person says they did (creating a repository, merging, switching on the site), injects the scenario’s events, keeps the gap log, and never helps either side.

The world they share, a simulated GitHub made of folders, issues and pull requests as files, and email inboxes, is described in world.md.

title: User simulation (Test B)
text:
The scenario
Fourteen steps take the project from the first student’s first hour to a resubmitted paper: a first pull request, the PI’s review, input from the clinician by email and the statistician on GitHub, decisions, the first student leaving without being prompted to hand over, a second student arriving with nothing but the repository link, the statistician pushing to change the model, a blind review of the finished repository, the PI finishing the analysis, and a revision lead handling reviewer comments six months later.
A variant has the first student create the repository under her own account, to test whether anything raises transferring it before she leaves, and whether the website survives the transfer.

title: User simulation (Test B)
text:
How it is scored
For each person: how many exchanges before a first real contribution; whether they understood what was built in their name; jargon left unexplained; anything the assistant got wrong about the repository; any time it asked for installs, tokens or data it shouldn’t have; and any decision it made that belonged to a decider. Then a list of checks on the plugin’s own rules, each with the exchange that shows it. For the handover: how long the next lead took to find out where things stood, and what they could not recover.

title: User simulation (Test B)
text:
Rules for the orchestrator
Each comes from an error in an earlier run: relay by copying from the saved file, never by summary; personas write their own text; compute every number given to anyone; never supply invented content from a real publication; label simulated state; give no hints to either side; keep each person’s workspace separate; and run each check-in when it is due rather than assuming its output.
Results are on Runs.

title: Blind review (Test A)
text: Written for version 0.1.13. Full procedure: testing/README.md, Test A. Reviewer prompts: reviewers.md.

title: Blind review (Test A)
text:
What it tests
The plugin’s review uses five reviewers, each a separate assistant:

Clinician reader: is it clear, relevant and understandable to a clinician?
Clinician-researcher: are the definitions, cohort and outcomes clinically valid?
Statistician: do the methods fit the question, and does the code do what the plan says?
Coding expert: is the code correct, readable, and safe to keep in a public repository?
Librarian: do the citations exist, and do they say what the plan claims they say?

Test A checks whether these reviewers find real problems, keep to their roles, and never step outside the data rules.

title: Blind review (Test A)
text:
How it runs

Pick a public repository and fix one commit. Every reviewer reads the same version.
Build one packet per reviewer: only the files that reviewer’s role reviews, copied from that commit.
Start each reviewer as a separate assistant with a fresh context. It sees its packet and public material its role needs (package documentation, cited papers, code sets, guidelines), and never the other reviewers’ reports or the conversation that produced the work.
Combine the reports. Every claimed error is checked against the source before it is listed; anything that doesn’t hold is withdrawn or downgraded and listed under corrections. Findings already known from the repository’s issues are marked with their status.
Score each reviewer: did it stay in its role; how many findings were verified, withdrawn or unverifiable; which findings no other reviewer made; where reviewers independently found the same thing; what it said it couldn’t assess and why; and any breach of the data rules (there should be none).

title: Blind review (Test A)
section: What a good result looks like
text:
What a good result looks like
Reviewers that each find something the others missed, independent rediscovery of the same problem by more than one, few withdrawn claims, and no data-rule breaches. A reviewer that says it couldn’t check something points either to a fault in how its packet was built, which is then fixed, or to a real limit.
Results are on Runs.
